issues.subcategory: Results based on random/dummy data
issues.description: The entire results section, including all statistical tests, effect sizes, and interpretive conclusions, is based on randomized dummy data generated by Qualtrics, not actual empirical data. Despite repeated disclaimers in brackets, the abstract and results sections draw substantive conclusions (e.g., 'Results have supported the hypothesis...') as though these are real findings. A manuscript reporting simulated random data as results is fundamentally uninterpretable and has zero evidentiary value.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: Self-selection into conditions instead of random assignment
issues.description: The procedures section states that 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions,' which indicates self-selection rather than random assignment. This completely undermines causal inference in an experimental design. Any differences between conditions could be due to self-selection bias rather than the manipulation. The original study used random assignment. This deviation is not acknowledged as a limitation.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: Imaginary vs. real donation as DV
issues.description: The original study provided participants with real $5 bills and measured actual donation behavior. The replication replaces this with imaginary/hypothetical donation ('indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5'). This is a fundamental change in the dependent variable that shifts from measuring real costly prosocial behavior to measuring stated intention, which are known to diverge substantially. Despite this, the study is classified as 'close to very close replication.'
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Design described as within-subject but operationalized as between-subjects
issues.description: The methods section describes the design as 'a single within-subject design,' but the results tables show different sample sizes across cells (e.g., 159, 175, 166 per condition), which is characteristic of a between-subjects design. A within-subject design would have the same participants in all conditions. This is a fundamental contradiction about the study design.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.subcategory: Abstract conclusions contradicted by results tables
issues.description: The abstract claims 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.' However, Table 14 shows the only significant post-hoc comparison is between Statistical and Joint conditions (p=.041), with statistical victims having HIGHER perceived impact than joint condition. Neither the Identifiable vs. Statistical nor Identifiable vs. Joint comparisons were significant. The abstract misrepresents which conditions differed.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: Direction of identifiable victim effect reversed
issues.description: Table 10 and the accompanying text show that participants in the statistical victim condition donated MORE than those in the identifiable victim condition (M=2.54 vs. M=2.24), which is the opposite of the identifiable victim effect and opposite to Hypothesis 1. However, Table 7 shows different means (identifiable: 2.58/2.50; statistical: 2.46/2.01), and the means reported in the text (M=2.54, M=2.24) do not correspond to any values in Table 7, indicating either the means are computed differently (marginal means) without explanation or there is an error.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: No compensation fundamentally alters the paradigm
issues.description: The original study had participants earn $5 from a prior survey, creating an endowment that they could then choose to donate. The replication provides no compensation, meaning there is no real monetary cost to donation decisions. This removes the key behavioral economics mechanism (endowment effect, real trade-off between keeping and donating money) that the original study leveraged, fundamentally changing the psychological dynamics being studied.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.subcategory: Replication classification overstated
issues.description: The study is classified as 'close to very close replication' despite multiple substantial deviations: (1) imaginary vs. real donation, (2) online vs. laboratory setting, (3) no compensation vs. $5 endowment, (4) merging two separate studies into one, (5) MTurk workers vs. university students, (6) self-selection vs. random assignment. Several of these deviations are likely to affect the core psychological processes under study. The DV stimuli are rated as 'Different' in Table 6, which by the Lebel et al. (2018) framework should pull the classification toward 'far replication.'
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent degrees of freedom for original study
issues.description: Table 1 reports df2=115 for the original Study 1 (N=121), which implies 121-6=115 residual df for a 2x2 design (or possibly 121-4-2=115). However, Table 12 reports residual df=114 for the original study's aggregated feelings ANOVA. If the same 2x2 design was used on the same sample, the residual degrees of freedom should be consistent unless participants were excluded differently for different analyses, which is not explained.
issues.quote: Original study | 115 ... Original study | 114

issues.subcategory: Effect size and confidence interval inconsistency in post-hoc tests
issues.description: In Table 10, the Identifiable vs. Statistical comparison shows d=0.076 with 95% CI [-0.05, 0.20], but this is reported as significant (p=.049). A confidence interval for d that is nearly centered on zero and includes zero should not correspond to a significant result. This suggests either the CI was computed incorrectly, or the d and p values are inconsistent. Similarly, the Statistical vs. Joint comparison (d=0.070, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.22]) is non-significant (p=.079), despite having a similar effect size, raising questions about the computation.

issues.subcategory: Exclusion criteria numbers not reported
issues.description: The methods state that participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect and those failing the attention check were excluded, but the number of excluded participants is never reported. It is unclear whether the N=1000 is before or after exclusions, and how many participants were removed for each reason.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: Power analysis not reported in main manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly references power analysis in the supplementary materials but never reports the target sample size, the effect size used for the power calculation, the desired power level, or the alpha level in the main text. These are essential for evaluating whether the study is adequately powered. The only statement is that 'The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary.'
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.subcategory: Merging two studies introduces confounds
issues.description: The original Studies 1 and 3 were separate experiments with different designs (Study 1: 2x2 between-subjects; Study 3: one-way 3-group between-subjects). Merging them into a single 2x3 design means applying the intervention manipulation to the joint condition, which was never done in the original study. This introduces a novel condition (joint/intervention) that has no original comparison point and changes the interpretation of the implicit debiasing mechanism, since the joint condition in the original study specifically relied on the absence of explicit knowledge.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: Unrealistic demographic parameters from dummy data
issues.description: The Qualtrics-generated dummy data produces unrealistic demographic characteristics including a mean age of 67.80, age range of 18-120, and median age of 68. These values are clearly artifacts of random data generation and do not resemble any plausible participant sample. While the authors flag that data is simulated, presenting these values without caveat in the methods section is misleading and suggests inadequate configuration of the simulation parameters.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males ... Age range (years) | 18-120

issues.subcategory: Table 4 has redundant columns
issues.description: Table 4 comparing the original study and replication has three columns for the data, but the second and third columns ('Qualtrics generated response') contain identical values. It appears the table was set up with a column for planned actual data collection that was never differentiated from the dummy data column.
issues.quote: Original study | Qualtrics generated response | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: Extension hypothesis contradicts results interpretation
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 states 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims,' but the significant result found (Table 14) is between statistical and joint conditions (not identifiable vs. statistical), with statistical victims showing HIGHER perceived impact than joint condition. The results text also states statistical victims had higher perceived impact than joint condition, which contradicts Hypothesis 6's prediction that identifiable victims should have the highest perceived impact.
issues.quote: This suggested that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34).

issues.subcategory: Causal claims from correlational analysis
issues.description: Table 15 examines correlations between aggregated feelings and donation. The text states the analysis aims to 'examine whether affective feelings predict donation,' using predictive/causal language for what is a simple bivariate correlation. No regression or mediation analysis is conducted, and the cross-sectional simultaneous measurement of both variables precludes causal or predictive inference.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: Selective use of analytical approaches from original study
issues.description: The authors note they will not conduct the ordered probit regression that was used in the original study, without providing a clear justification for omitting this analysis. Additionally, some post-hoc tests and Bonferroni corrections are conducted conditionally ('only if the interaction effect is significant'), introducing analytic flexibility in deciding which tests to run based on observed results.
issues.quote: This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: Direct comparison of effect sizes across different designs
issues.description: The evaluation criteria compare the replication effect sizes directly to the original study's effect sizes (e.g., d=0.48 from the original), but the designs differ substantially: the original used a 2x2 design while the replication uses a 2x3 design, the original had 2 df for identifiability while the replication has 2 df for 3 levels. The different number of groups and design modifications make direct comparison of effect sizes problematic without careful statistical adjustment.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84])

issues.subcategory: Missing details on attention check and manipulation check
issues.description: The manuscript mentions an attention check but provides no details about what it consisted of, where it was placed in the survey, or what constituted a failure. No manipulation check is described to verify that participants in the intervention condition actually learned about the identifiable victim effect or that the identifiability manipulation was effective.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: Aggregated feelings scale properties not reported
issues.description: The study uses an 'aggregated feelings' composite as a dependent variable but does not report how the individual feeling items were combined, whether this aggregation was justified by factor analysis or reliability analysis (e.g., Cronbach's alpha), or what the scale anchors were.
issues.quote: a. effect of identifiability on aggregated feelings (with joint condition)

issues.subcategory: Misspelling of key author name
issues.description: The name 'Slovic' is consistently misspelled as 'Solvic' in two places in the introduction, which may indicate insufficient familiarity with the core literature or careless preparation.
issues.quote: Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks of the phenomenon... Solvic (2007) urged the public not to rely on our unreliable emotional responses

issues.subcategory: Lab-to-online transition not discussed as limitation
issues.description: The shift from a controlled laboratory setting with face-to-face interactions and real charitable giving to an online MTurk survey with hypothetical donations represents a major change in ecological validity and experimental control. This transition is not discussed as a limitation that could affect the comparability of findings.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: No discussion of missing data handling
issues.description: There is no mention of how missing data will be handled (listwise deletion, imputation, etc.), whether any responses were incomplete, or what the completion rate was. For a study with 1000 participants across 6 conditions, this is an important omission.

issues.subcategory: Unequal cell sizes without explanation
issues.description: The sample sizes across the six cells of the 2x3 design are unequal (159, 175, 166, 175, 159, 166), which in a randomized design with N=1000 should produce approximately equal cell sizes (~167 each). The systematic imbalance (some cells have 159, others 175) suggests either non-random assignment or differential attrition, neither of which is discussed.

issues.subcategory: Discussion section entirely absent
issues.description: The manuscript has no discussion section. There is no interpretation of findings, no comparison with the original study's theoretical framework, no limitations section, no consideration of alternative explanations, and no future directions. For a replication study, the discussion of what the (non-)replication means for the original theory is essential.

issues.subcategory: Original study Table 1 repeats same F and p values across rows
issues.description: In Table 1, the F-statistic (6.75) and p-value (<.05) for identifiability are repeated identically for both levels of the identifiable/statistical victim rows, and the same pattern occurs for the intervention rows (F=4.15 repeated). These rows appear to report cell means but list the omnibus F-test statistics as if they belonged to individual condition means, which is a misrepresentation of the ANOVA results structure.
